01_tensors_shapes.title: Tensors, Scalars, Vectors, and Shapes
01_tensors_shapes.description:
Most ML code manipulates tensors with shapes. A scalar has shape `()`, a vector has one axis, and a matrix has two axes.

```python
vector = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
```

Shape reasoning is the base layer for everything else.

q2.question: Why do shapes matter in ML code?
options: They only matter for plotting charts.
They determine which operations are valid and how data flows through layers.
They replace the need for model parameters.
explanations: Shapes matter much more broadly than plotting.
Correct. Shape compatibility determines whether operations make sense.
Parameters are still needed.
q2.answerReason: A huge amount of ML debugging is really shape debugging.

q3.question: What is the main conceptual difference between a scalar and a vector?
options: A scalar is a single value; a vector is an ordered collection along one axis.
A scalar always lives on the CPU while a vector always lives on the GPU.
A vector cannot contain numbers.
explanations: Correct. Scalars and vectors differ by dimensional structure.
Device placement is a separate concern.
Vectors are usually numeric collections.
q3.answerReason: Before model architecture, you need a clear mental model of the data structures being transformed.

02_vector_dot.title: Dot Products as Weighted Similarity
02_vector_dot.description:
Many ML computations reduce to weighted sums, and the dot product is the simplest example.

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [3, 4]
```

Multiply aligned components and sum the results.

q2.question: Why does the dot product appear constantly in ML models?
options: It forms the weighted-sum scoring core of linear layers and similarity calculations.
It is only used for image resizing.
It always produces probabilities.
explanations: Correct. Weighted sums and alignment scores show up everywhere.
It is far broader than image resizing.
Dot products are not probabilities by themselves.
q2.answerReason: Linear models and neural layers are built on this weighted-combination idea.

q3.question: Why is the dot product a natural operation for a linear model?
options: Because it removes the need for weights.
Because it combines feature values and weights into one score.
Because it normalizes all features automatically.
explanations: Weights are still part of the computation.
Correct. Dot product is exactly a weighted sum across aligned dimensions.
Normalization is a separate operation.
q3.answerReason: A linear model asks: how much should each feature contribute to the score? The dot product answers that directly.

03_perceptron.title: Perceptrons, Weights, and Bias
03_perceptron.description:
A perceptron computes a weighted sum and shifts it with a bias.

```python
score = w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + bias
```

That score is then interpreted through a threshold or activation.

q2.question: What role does the bias play?
options: It shifts the decision boundary without changing the raw input features.
It sorts the training data before learning.
It removes the need for weights.
explanations: Correct. Bias offsets the activation score.
Sorting is unrelated.
Weights are still essential.
q2.answerReason: Bias lets the model activate even when inputs are zero or stay off despite positive weighted input.

q3.question: What role do the weights play?
options: They exist only for pretty printing the model.
They scale how strongly each input contributes to the score.
They force all inputs to contribute equally.
explanations: Weights participate directly in the computation, not just reporting.
Correct. Weight magnitude changes each feature’s influence.
Equal contribution would defeat learned weighting.
q3.answerReason: Weights express feature importance by controlling how much each input moves the score.

04_linear_regression_loss.title: Predictions Need a Loss Function
04_linear_regression_loss.description:
A model output becomes trainable only once you compare it with a target through a loss.

```python
loss = (prediction - target) ** 2
```

For regression, squared error is a common starting point.

q2.question: Why is a loss function needed?
options: To convert tensors into strings.
To replace model parameters.
To measure how wrong the prediction is so learning has a direction.
explanations: Formatting is unrelated.
Parameters still exist.
Correct. Without a loss, there is no objective to improve.
q2.answerReason: A model can produce numbers, but training needs a quantitative notion of error.

q3.question: What does squared error emphasize?
options: Larger prediction mistakes become disproportionately more costly.
All mistakes cost exactly the same.
Only positive mistakes count.
explanations: Correct. Squaring magnifies larger residuals.
Squared error is not constant-cost.
Negative residuals also matter once squared.
q3.answerReason: The shape of the loss influences how strongly optimization reacts to different kinds of mistakes.

05_gradient_descent.title: Gradient Descent Moves Downhill
05_gradient_descent.description:
If the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, subtracting it moves parameters downhill locally.

```python
weight = weight - lr * grad
```

q1.question: What is printed after one update?

q2.question: Why do we subtract the gradient during minimization?
options: Because gradients are always negative.
Because the gradient points toward increasing loss.
Because subtraction makes training deterministic.
explanations: Gradients can be positive, negative, or zero.
Correct. Moving opposite the gradient is the local downhill move.
Determinism depends on other factors too.
q2.answerReason: The sign of the update matters because we want to reduce the loss, not increase it.

q3.question: What does the learning rate control?
options: Whether gradients exist at all.
Whether the loss is convex.
How large each parameter update step is.
explanations: Gradients come from the model and loss.
Convexity is a property of the objective landscape.
Correct. The learning rate scales the step size.
q3.answerReason: Too small can slow learning; too large can overshoot or destabilize updates.

06_backprop_chain_rule.title: Backpropagation Uses the Chain Rule
06_backprop_chain_rule.description:
Deep networks are compositions of functions, so gradients are propagated backward using the chain rule.

```text
if z = f(y) and y = g(x), then dz/dx depends on dz/dy and dy/dx
```

Backprop is structured gradient bookkeeping across the computation graph.

q2.question: Why is the chain rule central to backpropagation?
options: Because model outputs depend on nested intermediate computations.
Because it alphabetizes parameters before training.
Because it removes the need for a loss function.
explanations: Correct. Composed functions require composed derivatives.
Alphabetical ordering is unrelated.
Loss is still required.
q2.answerReason: Neural nets are built from layers, so gradients must pass through one transformation after another.

q3.question: What is backprop fundamentally computing?
options: Only the final prediction.
How each parameter influenced the final loss through intermediate operations.
A new training dataset.
explanations: Prediction happens in the forward pass.
Correct. Backprop traces influence backward through the graph.
Backprop computes gradients, not data.
q3.answerReason: Training works because parameter updates depend on each parameter’s contribution to error.

07_relu_sigmoid.title: Activations Add Nonlinearity
07_relu_sigmoid.description:
Without nonlinear activations, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear transformation.

```python
relu = max(0, x)
```

ReLU and sigmoid serve different purposes and have different gradient behavior.

q2.question: Why are activation functions needed in neural networks?
options: To sort the training data.
To eliminate model parameters.
To let the network represent nonlinear relationships.
explanations: Sorting is unrelated.
Parameters still matter.
Correct. Nonlinearity is what makes deep networks more expressive than one linear layer.
q2.answerReason: Without nonlinear activations, depth does not buy the expressive behavior people want from neural networks.

q3.question: Why is ReLU often popular in practice?
options: It is simple and avoids the severe saturation behavior of sigmoid in many regions.
It converts any model into a probability distribution.
It guarantees perfect gradients everywhere.
explanations: Correct. ReLU’s piecewise behavior is simple and effective in many settings.
Probabilities require something like sigmoid/softmax depending on the task.
ReLU still has zero-gradient regions.
q3.answerReason: Activation choice affects optimization behavior, not just output range.

08_softmax_cross_entropy.title: Softmax and Cross-Entropy
08_softmax_cross_entropy.description:
Softmax turns logits into a normalized distribution, and cross-entropy measures how well that distribution matches the target class.

```python
probs = exp(logits) / sum(exp(logits))
```

q2.question: Why do larger logits get larger softmax probabilities?
options: Softmax sorts classes alphabetically first.
Exponentiation preserves ordering and amplifies score differences before normalization.
Softmax clips all logits to the same value.
explanations: Class names do not control probability.
Correct. Bigger logits create bigger exponentials before normalization.
Softmax does not flatten every class equally.
q2.answerReason: Normalization rescales, but the exponential step is what lets high logits dominate more strongly.

q3.question: Why is softmax commonly paired with cross-entropy for multiclass classification?
options: Because softmax alone trains the model automatically.
Because cross-entropy removes the need for logits.
Because one produces class probabilities and the other scores how wrong those probabilities are against the target.
explanations: Softmax does not provide a training objective by itself.
Cross-entropy is defined over predicted probabilities/logits relationships, not instead of them.
Correct. Prediction distribution and training objective play complementary roles.
q3.answerReason: You need both a way to express class confidence and a way to punish incorrect confidence.

09_tokenization.title: Tokenization Before Modeling
09_tokenization.description:
Language models do not ingest raw strings directly. Text is broken into tokens, and tokens map to integer ids.

```text
"hello world" -> [token ids]
```

Tokenization choice affects vocabulary size, efficiency, and what the model must learn.

q2.question: Why does tokenization matter before training an LLM?
options: The model needs discrete units it can embed, score, and predict.
It is only for pretty-printing outputs.
It removes the need for a vocabulary.
explanations: Correct. Tokenization defines the discrete symbols the model operates over.
Tokenization is part of the modeling pipeline, not just output formatting.
Tokenization and vocabulary are tightly connected.
q2.answerReason: Before embeddings or attention, the model needs a workable discrete representation of text.

q3.question: What tradeoff does tokenization influence?
options: Only GPU fan speed.
Vocabulary size, sequence length, and what kinds of patterns can be represented compactly.
Whether gradients exist.
explanations: Hardware fan speed is irrelevant.
Correct. Token granularity has real modeling and efficiency consequences.
Gradients are a training property, not a tokenizer property.
q3.answerReason: Different tokenizers change how much structure the model sees in each symbol and how long sequences become.

10_embeddings.title: Embeddings Turn Token Ids into Vectors
10_embeddings.description:
A token id by itself is just an index. An embedding layer turns that index into a learned dense vector.

```text
token id -> embedding lookup -> vector
```

Those vectors become the model’s starting representation of language units.

q2.question: Why is an embedding layer needed?
options: Because token ids are already meaningful geometric vectors.
Because it converts gradients into text.
Because the model needs learned continuous representations rather than treating ids as raw numeric magnitudes.
explanations: Token ids are arbitrary identifiers, not geometry by themselves.
Embeddings are about representation, not direct text conversion.
Correct. Learned vectors give the model a useful space for similarity and composition.
q2.answerReason: Embedding lookup is the bridge from discrete symbols to continuous model computation.

q3.question: Why would using raw token ids directly be a bad representation?
options: The numeric closeness of ids is arbitrary and does not represent semantic similarity.
Ids are always too large to fit in memory.
Raw ids automatically create attention weights.
explanations: Correct. Id numbers are labels, not learned meaning.
Memory is not the main conceptual issue here.
Attention needs vector representations to compare meaningfully.
q3.answerReason: Embeddings let the model learn structure instead of inheriting meaningless integer distances.

11_attention_scores.title: Attention Scores from Query-Key Alignment
11_attention_scores.description:
Self-attention begins by comparing a query vector with key vectors.

```python
score = q @ k
```

Larger scores usually mean the token is more relevant to the current query context.

q2.question: What does a larger query-key score usually mean?
options: The query is more aligned with that key, so that token can receive more attention weight.
The sequence becomes shorter.
The model skips the value vectors entirely.
explanations: Correct. Scores rank relevance before normalization.
Attention scores do not change sequence length directly.
Values are still needed for the final weighted mix.
q2.answerReason: The score is not the output itself; it is the relevance signal used to compute weights.

q3.question: Why are raw attention scores usually followed by softmax?
options: To remove the need for value vectors.
To change keys into labels.
To turn relative relevance scores into normalized attention weights.
explanations: Values are still needed after scoring.
Scores are not labels.
Correct. Softmax converts scores into a usable weighting distribution.
q3.answerReason: Raw comparisons become useful mixing coefficients only after normalization.

12_scaled_masked_attention.title: Scaling and Masking in Attention
12_scaled_masked_attention.description:
Transformers usually scale attention scores and may apply masks before softmax.

```text
scaled scores = (QK^T) / sqrt(d_k)
```

Scaling stabilizes score magnitude, and masking can block future positions or padding tokens.

q2.question: Why divide attention scores by `sqrt(d_k)`?
options: To convert the model into a CNN.
To keep score magnitudes from growing too large as key/query dimension increases.
To remove the need for softmax.
explanations: Architecture type is unrelated.
Correct. Large dot products can make softmax too peaky and gradients less stable.
Softmax is still used.
q2.answerReason: Score scaling is a numerical-stability trick tied to vector dimensionality.

q3.question: What is the purpose of a causal mask in an autoregressive decoder?
options: It prevents a position from attending to future tokens that should not be visible yet.
It forces every token to attend equally to all previous tokens.
It removes tokenization from the model.
explanations: Correct. Autoregressive training/generation requires hiding future information.
Masks constrain visibility, not equalize weights.
Tokenization is a separate preprocessing stage.
q3.answerReason: Without a causal mask, next-token prediction training would leak future information backward into earlier positions.

13_multi_head_attention.title: Why Multi-Head Attention Exists
13_multi_head_attention.description:
A single attention mechanism can focus on one pattern. Multiple heads let the model project into multiple subspaces and capture different relationships in parallel.

```text
head1, head2, ... -> concatenate -> mix
```

q2.question: Why use multiple attention heads instead of only one?
options: To eliminate the need for embeddings.
To make every head compute the same pattern redundantly.
To let the model capture different kinds of relationships in parallel subspaces.
explanations: Embeddings are still required.
The point is diversity, not redundancy.
Correct. Different heads can specialize in different signal patterns.
q2.answerReason: Multi-head attention increases representational flexibility by letting attention look from multiple angles.

q3.question: What happens after the per-head attention outputs are computed?
options: They are deleted immediately.
They are combined, typically by concatenation followed by a learned projection.
They are turned into tokenizer rules.
explanations: The outputs are used, not discarded.
Correct. Multi-head structure eventually merges back into one representation stream.
Tokenization is a separate stage.
q3.answerReason: Heads are useful because their outputs are recombined into a richer joint representation.

14_transformer_block.title: Residuals, Norms, and Feed-Forward Blocks
14_transformer_block.description:
A transformer block is more than attention alone. It typically includes attention, residual connections, normalization, and a position-wise feed-forward network.

```python
x = x + attention_delta
```

Residual paths help preserve signal while later sublayers refine it.

q2.question: Why are residual connections important in deep transformer stacks?
options: They let layers learn corrections on top of existing representations instead of rebuilding everything from scratch.
They remove the need for any nonlinear operations.
They force every layer to compute the exact same function.
explanations: Correct. Residual learning improves optimization and information flow.
Residuals complement, not replace, nonlinear layers and normalization.
Layers can still learn very different transformations.
q2.answerReason: Residual paths help deep networks preserve useful signal while adding refinements gradually.

q3.question: Why is the feed-forward network still important even after attention?
options: Because attention cannot produce vectors.
Because it tokenizes the input again.
Because attention mixes information across positions, while the feed-forward sublayer applies learned nonlinear transformation at each position.
explanations: Attention does produce vector outputs.
The transformer does not re-tokenize here.
Correct. The block needs both cross-position mixing and per-position transformation capacity.
q3.answerReason: Attention is not the whole transformer; the feed-forward part adds substantial modeling power too.

15_batches_optimizer.title: Mini-Batches, Optimizers, and Gradient Reset
15_batches_optimizer.description:
Training rarely uses one example at a time for large models. Mini-batches improve throughput, and optimizers update parameters from accumulated gradients.

```python
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
```

q2.question: Why is `zero_grad()` part of many training loops?
options: Because backpropagation deletes the model after each batch.
Because gradients often accumulate unless you clear them before the next step.
Because it chooses a new architecture each iteration.
explanations: The model is not deleted after each batch.
Correct. Stale accumulated gradients can corrupt the intended update.
Architecture search is unrelated.
q2.answerReason: Many frameworks accumulate gradients by default, so reset behavior matters.

q3.question: Why use mini-batches instead of one example at a time for large training jobs?
options: They improve hardware utilization and provide a more efficient gradient estimate per optimizer step.
They make loss functions unnecessary.
They guarantee perfect generalization.
explanations: Correct. Batching is about computational efficiency and gradient statistics.
Loss functions are still essential.
Generalization is not guaranteed by batching.
q3.answerReason: Batching is part of the systems side of training, not just the math side.

16_llm_next_token.title: Autoregressive Next-Token Prediction
16_llm_next_token.description:
An LLM does not emit one whole answer at once. It predicts a distribution over the next token, selects one token, appends it to context, and repeats.

```text
context -> logits -> probabilities -> next token -> longer context
```

q2.question: What is the model output immediately before token selection?
options: A vector of logits over the vocabulary.
A final paragraph string already fixed in full.
The dataset loss value.
explanations: Correct. Generation works one next-token distribution at a time.
Text is built token by token, not chosen as one finished paragraph in advance.
Training loss is not the direct generation output.
q2.answerReason: Logits are the per-step scoring output; decoding decides how one token is chosen from them.

q3.question: Why is next-token prediction such a powerful training objective for language models?
options: Because it memorizes one fixed answer per prompt length.
Because every token in text becomes a supervised target conditioned on its context, forcing the model to learn syntax, semantics, and long-range patterns.
Because it removes the need for an objective function.
explanations: Generalization is richer than memorizing one fixed answer for each length.
Correct. The text itself provides dense supervision step by step.
Next-token prediction is itself the objective.
q3.answerReason: Autoregressive prediction squeezes a huge amount of structure out of plain text because every position becomes training signal.
